title: The Cover Crisis Pulls Back
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer reflects on work after the LA fires, where a group studying community recovery concluded that by the time a crisis lands it is already too late to begin. Crises do not create our problems, she says, they only pull back the cover on cracks that were already there. She names three emerging practices: telling the truth plainly, slowing down enough to be present, and building what comes next on purpose. The central argument is that the leadership problem is not a lack of awareness but a reluctance to own what we already perceive, because speaking a truth changes who is responsible for what happens next. She locates the real threshold between clarity and choosing and calls out avoidance as a well-dressed way of postponing what feels hard. She argues this is not a case for bluntness as a weapon, and ends with reflection questions and a Baldwin quotation about facing what must be changed.
points: Disasters expose rather than invent weaknesses, so the time to strengthen communities and systems is before the crisis.
The leadership gap is rarely awareness; it is the unwillingness to say aloud what we already sense, because a spoken truth reassigns responsibility.
The real threshold is between seeing a truth and choosing to build a life or team around it.
Waiting for more time, information or certainty is often a polite form of avoidance that drains energy and erodes integrity.
Honest steps can be small: one sentence said without cushioning, one pattern stopped, one honest conversation.
quotes: By the time a crisis lands, it is already too late to begin. Fire, flood, collapse, none of it invents our problems, it only exposes what was already there.
Because the pattern underneath all of this isn’t a lack of awareness. It’s a reluctance to fully own what we already perceive.
But a truth once spoken takes on shape. It moves the conversation. It moves who is responsible for what happens next.
That is the real threshold, not between confusion and clarity, but between clarity and choosing. Seeing a truth is not the same as building a life around it.
More often it’s a well-dressed way of postponing what feels hard. And avoidance, however reasonable it looks from the outside, has a cost.
None of this is an argument for bluntness as a weapon, or certainty as a performance. It’s a call for letting reality be seen as it is because a thing has to be visible before it can be changed.
